newsitem.title: KENYA: Rwandan Hutus escape east Zaire conflict to Kenya.
newsitem.headline: Rwandan Hutus escape east Zaire conflict to Kenya.

text.p: Some 500 Rwandan Hutus, mainly family members of former Rwandan troops, have escaped to Kenya from a refugee camp in eastern Zaire using a secretive air route organised by Hutu businessmen, Hutu sources said on Wednesday.
They said many more from Tingi Tingi camp in eastern Zaire, which has some 170,000 Rwandan and Burundi refugees, would like to follow suit but were hindered by the $800 per person cost of the flight.
They said the Hutus were fleeing rebels of Laurent Kabila's Alliance of Democratic Forces for the Liberation of Congo-Zaire (ADFL) as they advance in the east towards refugee centres.

"Some 500 people have so far arrived in Kenya but none of them are of any political significance in the Rwandan context. Many are actually family members of the ousted army," a source in the Rwandan Hutu community in Kenya told Reuters.
"They are fleeing the heat caused by Kabila's advance on Zairean army positions and those of Rwanda's ousted army in the refugee camps in Zaire."
"The idea for many of them is to be in Kenya for a while before arranging documents to enable them travel to Europe and other parts of the world where they could resettle," he added.

But diplomats said among those coming out of eastern Zaire, where there are some 400,000 Rwandan and Burundian refugees, were officers in Rwanda's former Hutu army who fled Rwanda in fear of reprisals for the 1994 genocide of some 800,000 people.
They said between 30 and 40 former members of the former Rwandan Armed Forces (FAR) arrived in Nairobi on Tuesday and various embassies in the Kenyan capital were receiving requests for visas.
Kabila, whose forces have captured a large swath of eastern Zaire since October, had threatened to attack Tingi Tingi, saying it was a militarised zone harbouring armed members of the Hutu army.
But he said earlier this month that he would hold off to allow the U.N. refugee agency time to try to separate fighters from civilian refugees.
Former Rwandan Hutu soldiers have fought alongside Zaire's ragged and retreating army in Africa's latest conflict.

"But many of them no longer want to take part in a war that is not theirs. This is why there is a growing mood for them to leave Zaire and resettle elsewhere," said Seth Sendashonga, an exiled Hutu politician and former Rwandan interior minister.

Sendashonga told Reuters he approached the United States, France and Belgium last year to try to persuade them to join a scheme to return the Hutus to Rwanda in return for guarantees for their safety.

"The idea was for these western powers to act as guarantors of safety for the returning Hutus. Because Rwanda is far better place for the Hutus than war-torn Zaire," said Sendashonga, adding that he had never received a response from the powers.
"I was hoping to give the Hutus trapped in Zaire a way out and also the international community an acceptable solution to scale down tension in the region," Sendashonga added.
He said he now doubted whether his earlier plan could now work because of reports that some Hutu former army officers who returned had disappeared in Rwanda and others were killed.

The London-based human rights group Amnesty International said a week ago unlawful executions by the Rwanda Patriotic Army (RPA) had increased this year especially in reprisal operations after attacks.
Rwanda's army denied carrying out any unlawful executions.
Amnesty also reported Tutsi civilians were being killed by former Rwandan Hutu soldiers or militiamen who returned with more than a million Hutu refugees from Tanzania and Zaire late last year.
